newsitem.title: JAPAN: Key points Japan securities panel Big Bang report.
newsitem.headline: Key points Japan securities panel Big Bang report.

text.p: Following are the main points of a final report released by Japan's Securities and Exchange Council, an advisory panel to the Finance Minister, proposing deregulation of Japan's securities markets.
The wide-ranging proposals were made to help Japan set a schedule for implementing its "Big Bang" financial market reforms.
The report from the panel will be adopted as is by the ministry, financial sources said.
*Japan should completely liberalise commissions on stock transactions by the end of calendar 1999.
*Liberalisation of stock broking fees from April 1998, should initially cover only stock transactions of more than 50 million yen, so as to smooth the transition to a deregulated environment.
*Japan should abolish the licencing system for brokers engaging in the securities business.

*Japan should adopt a registration system to open up the securities business to new participants, although in highly specialised businesses, such as underwriting and over-the-counter derivatives dealing, approval from regulators should continue to be required.

*Banks' securities units should be allowed to engage in stock broking in the second half of the 1999/2000 business year. They should be permitted to enter all securities businesses except stock broking in the latter half of 1997/98.

*Harsher penalties should be imposed against illegal stock transactions, such as insider trading and stock manipulation, in line with global standards, and staff levels should be increased at Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), to improve its market-monitoring operations. A Finance Ministry official said the ministry may submit a bill to revise the Securities and Exchange Act to an extraordinary parliamentary session expected in this autumn.
*Tax authorities should consider abolishing securities transaction taxes to improve the efficiency of Japan's securities markets and to cut trading costs to internationally competitive levels.
*Brokerages should be allowed to make transactions involving listed stocks outside Japan's eight stock exchanges, in order to step up competition.

*Securities houses should be allowed to start offering multi-service accounts in the 1997/98 business year to enable customers to transfer profits automatically from stock sales into money management funds.

*Securities houses should be allowed to offer "wrap" accounts, widely used in the United States, in which a securities house manages an investor's assets based on discretionary management contracts or by introducing third-party advisory firms to investors.
*Mechanisms should be enshrined in the law to prevent customers from losing their money if deregulation pushes brokerages into bankruptcy.
*Rules that restrict brokers from engaging in businesses such as asset management, investment trusts, insurance and commodities futures should be abolished.
*Financial institutions, such as banks, should be allowed to start over-the-counter sales of investment trusts so as to make Japan's investment trust funds more attractive to investors.
*Introduction of privately placed investment trusts should be permitted for a limited number of investors.

The ministry official said the bills should be submitted to the next ordinary session of parliament expected to start next January in order to implement the proposed reforms that require revisions to the Securities and Exchange Law.
